lessons.title: One word, several pieces
lessons.goal: See how small words join onto the front and back of an Arabic word, and how Bayan shows the pieces.

blocks.md: In English, "and in the hereafter" is four words. In Arabic it is **one**: the small words for "and", "in" and "the" are joined onto the front of the noun.

Every Arabic word has a **main body** (the stem, which carries the meaning) and can have **prefixes** before it and **suffixes** after it. {{stat:affix_pct}} of the {{stat:words}} words in the Qur'an carry at least one of them, so learning these pieces pays off on almost every line.
Tap any example to open its Bayan page. The top of the page splits the word into **PREFIX**, **MAIN BODY** and **SUFFIX**, with a card explaining each piece.

quiz.q: How many English words is وَبِٱلْءَاخِرَةِ?
quiz.explain: وَ + بِ + ٱلْ + ءَاخِرَة = "and in the Hereafter".

quiz.q: Which part of a word carries its main meaning?
quiz.explain: The stem carries the meaning; prefixes and suffixes add small words like "and", "the" or "their".

quiz.q: In خَلَقَكُمْ, what does ـكُمْ add?
quiz.explain: ـكُمْ is the pronoun "you" (plural): "He created you".

lessons.title: وَ "and" and فَ "so"
lessons.goal: Recognise the two most common joined words and the oath meaning of وَ.

blocks.md: **وَ (wa) "and"** is the most common prefix in the Qur'an — it appears {{stat:waw}} times. It is never written on its own; it always joins the next word.
At the start of a sūrah, وَ before a noun often means **"By ...!"** — an oath:

items.note: Sūrat al-ʿAṣr opens with an oath.
ض is a sun letter too.

blocks.md: **فَ (fa) "so, then"** links two things in order, or shows a result. It appears {{stat:fa}} times.

items.note: One thing happened, then the next.
Yaʿqūb's reply in 12:18: فَ shows what follows from what came before.

blocks.md: Read the vowel too: وَ and فَ always have a fatḥa. A word that starts with و or ف with another vowel (e.g. فِي "in") is not this prefix.

quiz.q: What does وَٱلْعَصْرِ mean at the start of Sūrat al-ʿAṣr?
quiz.explain: At the opening of a sūrah, وَ before a noun is an oath: "By the time!"

quiz.q: What does فَ usually add?
quiz.explain: فَ links things in sequence or shows a result.

quiz.q: Is the فِ in فِي ("in") the prefix فَ?
options: No — it has a kasra, and فِي is a word of its own
quiz.explain: The prefix is always فَ with a fatḥa. فِي is a separate word, "in".

lessons.title: بِ "with", لِ "for", كَ "like"
lessons.goal: Recognise the three joined prepositions and what they do to the word after them.

blocks.md: Three short prepositions are always written joined to the next word:

items.note: بِ + ٱسْم; the ٱ of ٱسْم drops out after بِ.
لِ + ٱللَّه: the ٱ drops out, and rather than three ل's in a row only two are written, the second with a shadda.

blocks.md: A noun after بِ, لِ or كَ usually ends in **-i** (kasra or -in): bi-smi, lillāhi, bil-qalami, ka-mathali. This ending is the genitive case, and it's a quick way to spot that a preposition is at work.
Don't confuse لِ with **لَ (la), "surely, indeed"**, which has a fatḥa and adds emphasis:

quiz.q: What does بِٱلْقَلَمِ mean?
quiz.explain: بِ (by) + ٱلْ (the) + قَلَم (pen).

quiz.q: لِ + ٱللَّه would give three ل's in a row. Why does لِلَّهِ have only two?
options: The ٱ drops out, and the spelling writes the ل's as two, with a shadda
quiz.explain: After لِ the joining ٱ disappears. Three ل's in a row are never written, so لِلَّهِ has two: لِ, then لَّ with a shadda.

quiz.q: What ending does a noun take after بِ, لِ or كَ?
quiz.explain: These prepositions put the noun in the genitive, which usually ends in -i.

quiz.q: What does لَقَدْ mean?
quiz.explain: لَ with a fatḥa is emphatic: la-qad, "certainly".

lessons.title: "my, your, his": pronouns on nouns
lessons.goal: Read the pronoun endings that mean my, your, his, her, our and their.

blocks.md: Possessive words are suffixes joined to the end of the noun. The word رَبّ (Lord) shows almost all of them in the Qur'an:
**ـهُ becomes ـهِ after an i-sound** (kasra, ī or y). The meaning doesn't change:

items.note: Same meaning as رَبُّهُۥ — the kasra on ب turns -hū into -hī.

blocks.md: A noun with a pronoun ending never also has ٱلْ or tanwīn: it's already definite ("my Lord", not "a my Lord").

quiz.q: What does رَبُّنَا mean?
quiz.explain: ـنَا means "our".

quiz.q: What is the difference between رَبُّكَ and رَبُّكِ?
options: Speaking to a man vs speaking to a woman
quiz.explain: ـكَ is "your" to one man, ـكِ is "your" to one woman.

quiz.q: رَبُّهُمْ and رَبِّهِمْ both mean "their Lord". Why the different vowel?
options: ـهُمْ becomes ـهِمْ after an i-sound
quiz.explain: After a kasra, ī or y, the pronoun's ḍamma becomes a kasra: -hum → -him.

quiz.q: Can رَبُّنَا also take ٱلْ?
options: No — a pronoun ending already makes it definite
quiz.explain: A noun never has both ٱلْ and a pronoun ending.

lessons.title: "me, him, them": pronouns on verbs and prepositions
lessons.goal: Read object pronouns on verbs and pronouns on little words like لَ, فِي and عَلَى.

blocks.md: The same endings go on verbs, where they mean **who the action is done to** (the object). The only new one is **"me": ـنِى** on a verb (not ـِى).
Prepositions take the same endings:

items.note: لِ becomes لَ before a pronoun (except لِى, "for me"): la-hū.
عَلَى becomes عَلَيْـ before a pronoun.
إِلَى becomes إِلَيْـ before a pronoun.

blocks.md: عَلَى (on) and إِلَى (to) turn their final ى into يْ when a pronoun is added: عَلَيْهِمْ, إِلَيْكَ. Spot the يْ and you know there's a pronoun after it.

quiz.q: How do you say "He created me"?
quiz.explain: On a verb, "me" is ـنِى: khalaqanī.

quiz.q: What does ٱهْدِنَا mean?
quiz.explain: ٱهْدِ (guide!) + ـنَا (us).

quiz.q: What does عَلَيْهِمْ mean?
quiz.explain: عَلَى (on) + ـهِمْ (them); the ى becomes يْ.

quiz.q: Why is لِ written لَ in لَهُۥ?
options: لِ takes a fatḥa before a pronoun
quiz.explain: The preposition لِ becomes لَ before most pronouns: lahū, lahum, lakum.

lessons.title: When "my" is hidden
lessons.goal: Spot the pronoun "my" when the Qur'an doesn't write its ي.

blocks.md: Sometimes the ي of "my" isn't written as a letter of its own. There are three ways this happens.
**1. The ي is dropped and only a kasra is left.** This is common when calling out to someone:

items.note: Not qawmī: the ي is dropped, and the kasra under م is all that's left of "my".
Ibrāhīm calling on God: "My Lord, make this a secure city".

blocks.md: رَبِّ can also mean **"Lord of"**, with no "my" at all: رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ in 1:2 is "Lord of the worlds". The spelling is the same; the words around it tell you which it is.
**2. The ي merges into a shadda** when the word already ends in ي:

items.note: إِلَى → إِلَيْ + ي = إِلَيَّ: the two ي's are written as one with a shadda.

blocks.md: **3. A fatḥa is left instead**, in the set phrase "O son of my mother":

items.note: Hārūn speaking to Mūsā. The ي of "my" became an alif and was dropped, leaving the fatḥa on م.

blocks.md: On a word page Bayan shows a hidden "my" as a faded (ي) in the SUFFIX box, and the suffix card explains which of these three cases it is.

quiz.q: What does يَٰقَوْمِ mean?
quiz.explain: The kasra on م is what's left of the dropped "my".

quiz.q: Does رَبِّ always mean "my Lord"?
options: No — it can also mean "Lord of", as in رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ
quiz.explain: The spelling is the same; context decides between "my Lord" and "Lord of".

quiz.q: Where is the "my" in إِلَىَّ?
options: Merged into the shadda on ي
quiz.explain: The word's own ي and the ي of "my" are written as one ي with a shadda.
